title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the coupling's primary mechanical function.
student: What is the primary mechanical function of the flanged coupling in the rotating equipment system?
instructor: The coupling joins two rotating shafts and transfers torque from the driving machine to the driven machine while maintaining rotational continuity between them.

title: Source of Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the mechanical loading transmitted by the coupling.
student: What type of mechanical loading must the coupling transmit during normal operation?
instructor: The coupling must transmit torque generated by the driving machine to the driven equipment. This produces torsional loading in the shafts and shear loading in the coupling connection.

title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque through the physical coupling.
student: Trace the mechanical torque-transfer path from the driving machine to the driven machine.
instructor: Torque passes from the driving machine into the driving shaft, then into the first flange, through the coupling bolts to the mating flange, and finally into the driven shaft and driven machine.

title: Critical Mechanical Responses
learningObjectives: Identify components that experience significant shear stress.
student: Which components are expected to experience significant shear stress while torque is being transmitted?
instructor: The shafts experience torsional shear stress. The coupling bolts experience direct shear as they transfer torque between the two flanges.

title: Effect of Bolt Arrangement
learningObjectives: Explain how bolt count and radius affect force per bolt.
student: How would increasing the number of bolts or placing the bolts farther from the shaft centerline affect the force carried by each bolt?
instructor: More bolts distribute the transmitted torque among more connectors and reduce the force carried by each bolt. Moving the bolts farther from the shaft centerline increases their moment arm, so a smaller tangential force per bolt is required to transmit the same torque.

title: Relevant Geometric Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify geometry controlling shaft and bolt stresses.
student: What geometric characteristics of the shaft and bolt group would you expect to influence shaft stress and bolt shear stress?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include shaft size, number of bolts, bolt diameter, and radial location of the bolts relative to the shaft axis. These determine the shaft torsional resistance and the bolt-group torque capacity.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the physical coupling into a simplified mechanics model.
student: Convert the real flanged coupling into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the torque-transfer path. Show the two shafts, mating flanges, circular bolt group, transmitted torque, shaft size, bolt size, and bolt-pattern radius.
instructor: A suitable model contains two coaxial solid shafts connected by rigid flanges. Identical bolts are equally spaced on a circular bolt pattern. Torque enters through one shaft, is transferred through the bolt group, and exits through the other shaft.
gradingNotes: Students should create their own idealization before using the instructor reference figure.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions used in the simplified coupling model.
student: State the assumptions used to simplify the real coupling into the mechanics model.
instructor: Assume solid circular shafts, rigid flanges, identical equally spaced bolts, equal tangential load sharing among bolts, average direct shear for bolt stress, and static torque transmission. Neglect bolt preload and frictional torque transfer, bearing stress, flange flexure, fatigue, fit, and stress concentrations.
gradingNotes: The stress comparison used later is a prescribed MEEN 305 design criterion, not a complete industrial coupling-design standard.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the symbolic bolt-group design procedure.
student: Before performing the derivation, describe the sequence needed to determine the required bolt count.
instructor: Determine the maximum torsional shear stress in the shaft; use torque equilibrium of the bolt group to determine the force in each bolt; calculate average bolt shear stress; apply the prescribed stress-comparison criterion; solve symbolically for the required number of bolts; round up to a practical integer count; and verify the selected configuration.

title: Boundary Conditions and Torque Equilibrium
learningObjectives: Describe the loading representation and torque equilibrium.
student: From the instructor reference diagram, describe the loading representation and state the global torque equilibrium condition.
instructor: The two machine sides apply equal and opposite torques of magnitude T. Under steady torque transmission, the coupling transfers torque of magnitude T from one shaft to the other. For the assigned input, T = {{coupling_torque_Nmm}} N·mm.

title: Maximum Shear Stress in the Shaft
learningObjectives: Derive maximum torsional shear stress in a solid shaft.
student: Derive the maximum torsional shear stress in the solid circular shaft.
instructor: For a solid circular shaft, J = πr4/2. Therefore, τshaft,max = Tr/J = 2T/(πr3). The maximum occurs at the outer surface. For the assigned inputs, J = {{coupling_shaft_J_mm4}} mm4 and τshaft,max = {{coupling_shaft_tau_MPa}} MPa.

title: Tangential Force in Each Bolt
learningObjectives: Relate transmitted torque to force in each bolt.
student: Assuming equal load sharing among n bolts located at bolt-circle radius R, determine the tangential shear force carried by each bolt.
instructor: Torque equilibrium gives T = nFbR. Therefore, Fb = T/(nR). For the selected integer pattern, Fb = {{coupling_bolt_force_N}} N.

title: Average Shear Stress in Each Bolt
learningObjectives: Derive the average direct shear stress in a coupling bolt.
student: Determine the average direct shear stress in one coupling bolt.
instructor: The bolt shear area is Ab = πdb2/4 = {{coupling_bolt_area_mm2}} mm2. Thus, τb = Fb/Ab = 4T/(nπR db2). For the selected pattern, τb = {{coupling_bolt_tau_MPa}} MPa.

title: Required Number of Bolts
learningObjectives: Derive the theoretical required bolt count.
student: Apply the prescribed stress-comparison criterion and solve symbolically for the required number of bolts.
instructor: Using the limiting condition τb = τshaft,max, set 4T/(nπR db2) = 2T/(πr3). Solving gives nreq = 2r3/(R db2) = {{coupling_n_req}}. The transmitted torque and π cancel because both stresses scale linearly with torque.
gradingNotes: The equality is the limiting condition for this exercise. A selected integer configuration should satisfy τb ≤ τshaft,max.

title: Practical Integer Selection
learningObjectives: Convert the theoretical result into an implementable bolt count.
student: Convert the theoretical bolt count into an implementable bolt-group configuration.
instructor: Select nselected = ceil[2r3/(R db2)] = {{coupling_n_selected}} bolts. If a symmetric bolt pattern or manufacturing convention requires a larger count, choose the next acceptable pattern. Then verify that τb ≤ τshaft,max. {{coupling_stress_assessment}}

title: Sensitivity and Design Interpretation
learningObjectives: Interpret sensitivity using the symbolic bolt-count relation.
student: Explain how shaft radius, bolt-circle radius, and bolt diameter affect the required bolt count.
instructor: From nreq = 2r3/(R db2), the required bolt count scales with r3, inversely with R, and inversely with db2. A larger shaft radius increases the required count strongly under the prescribed criterion, while a larger bolt-circle radius or larger bolt diameter reduces it.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
student: Using the derived relation, state how the final bolt pattern should be selected and identify one limitation of the simplified model.
instructor:
{{coupling_recommendation}}

The simplified result does not constitute a complete coupling design because bolt preload, friction, fatigue, bearing, flange deformation, fit, keys or splines, and applicable coupling standards are not evaluated.
gradingNotes: The final recommendation should remain a limited mechanics-based selection rather than a claim of complete industrial design acceptance.
